title: Down the Ore Line
passages:
The back room was warm, which was the first wrong thing. The second was the man on Teodoro's couch, breathing.

Wren stopped inside the door. Rhea's knife had left her wrists bare and pale where the tape had been, and she rubbed one against the other without knowing she did it.

"Three," she said.

Marlowe looked at her. Gray around the mouth, one shoulder strapped down under a cargo-strap splint, the other arm laid across his stomach like something he was keeping from rolling off. He didn't say anything.

"Two."

That was the wall. She'd carried those two numbers since Bay 4, since the lid came down and Voss's stamp came down on the seal and her own voice went counting in her ears. She'd come four hundred kilometers and walked into a warm room to say the rest of it to the man in the box. The rest wouldn't come. There was nothing after two. She'd never let there be.

Marlowe's mouth worked. "Cup," he said.

"...What?"

"On the floor. By the couch leg." He didn't lift his head off the armrest. "I can get it if I go flat, and I can't go flat without this"—he meant the shoulder—"telling me about my life choices. So it's been down there since Teodoro went out to the board." A breath. "You've got two arms. I can see them from here."

Wren stared at him. She had rehearsed this in the dark of the tool void a hundred times. The accusation, the flinch, *something*. She had not rehearsed a water cup.

"You don't know who I am," she said.

"Should I?" His eyes closed. "You're the lid-hand. Slate says Bay 4. That's more name than I had two days ago, so congratulations, we're even."

"I counted you down."

"Did it work?"

"What?"

"Am I down?" One eye opened, wet and irritated. "Because I'm sitting up, and I'd like a drink, and I'd like it before the bell. So whatever you think you did, you did it bad."

Wren crouched and got the cup, a dented steel thing, half full, and put it in his working hand. He drank like it was the point of the whole business. To him, maybe it was.

From the doorway Coombs cleared his throat. He had the tender's remote in one fist and the proving slate under his arm, and he wore the patient look of a man paid by the settled thing.

"That's the remand," he said, nodding at her wrists like the tape was still on them. "You've all been reading it wrong." He came a step in, genial as a stove. "A hold order doesn't execute at a node. Can't. A node's a closed roster. You lift a body off a closed roster, now you've got two rosters out of balance and a desk that notices. It only executes where a coast line can take you off my hands clean." He let it sit. "One place on this line does that. The switch stand at the Weir. That's where your count gets settled, lid-hand. Not here. Here you're just a woman who wants to be heard." He tipped the slate toward the door, the dark, the ore line, the cold coming up off it. "Tender rolls at the bell. Whatever you're gonna say to him, say it on the way. After the switch it stops being yours to say."

Wren looked at Marlowe. Marlowe had his eyes shut again and the empty cup against his chest, gone somewhere a shoulder didn't hurt.

The bell was twenty-eight minutes out.

Outside, the cold took the warm room off Wren's face in one pull. Anza's ore stub was four lamps and a lot of dark, and the dead med rig sat under a tarp at the end of it with a clean square hole in its dash where the transponder used to be — the box that tells a board where a rig is, so the board can pretend to care.

"Wrists," Rhea said.

Wren put them out. Rhea pulled the roll of seal tape from her coat, gray and stiff with cold, printed every hand's width with a receiving mark: BAY 4 SHIFT 2, the code a bay stamps so anyone downstream can see whose hands took delivery. Three turns, pressed flat with her thumb, torn with her teeth.

"You're quick at that," Wren said.

"Forty times a shift. Tape is the only thing out here that doesn't change its story." Rhea cut the tail short and put it in her pocket instead of the bin. "You, on the other hand, cut a seal in a tool void with a seam knife."

"You'd have done it too, if you'd been the one holding the lid."

"I'd have said one," Rhea said. "There's three numbers. You stopped at two like the last one costs money."

"It does."

Teodoro had the board ledge open on his knees, keying with two fingers, breath going up around his face. "Slate carries you as Bay Four lid-hand," he said. "Hands with a bay number where a badge goes. That's a live entry, so nobody shoots you on sight, and it's good exactly as far as the switch, because past the switch a coast roster line takes a body off the slate and writes whatever it likes in the name field. I can't hold it longer. I tried the hold-order field and the field tried me back."

"Comforting," Wren said.

"You want comforting, go be cargo." He sealed the ledge. "Also your man in there refuses to countersign himself off the plate. I've asked twice. He said he's shop crew and shop crew doesn't quit before the bell."

Nour came out of the shop with the last spare cartridge in one fist — the little brass-throated canister that scrubs a respirator's air until the diaphragm quits — and the draw-line key in the other, the sprung brass handle that opens Anza's resupply draw and keeps the node's chain green.

"I'm not standing out here watching a tender leave," she said, and pushed the cartridge into Rhea's coat. "That's Ivo's. It goes in at minute forty or he starts sounding like a bad pump. I've got the draw. Nobody at this node eats until I say, and I say at shift change."

"Twenty-six minutes," Rhea said. "If the switch goes wrong—"

"Then be wrong somewhere with a knife and a name," Nour said, and went back in, and the shop door dropped and sealed behind her.

Miko was already up on the shelf over the motor box, boots braced against the coolant loop, arms wrapped round her knees, looking like a woman who had found the good seat on purpose.

"The Weir's the coast switch," she said, when she caught Wren looking. "Two years I've been buying my way to a green board. I'm not sitting out a night in a relay shop because somebody's got two numbers left to say."

"You're not coming back."

"Not to anything with a roster on it, no."

Coombs swung up onto the deck plate with the remote in his fist and thumbed it twice. The tender cranked over — a low shudder up through the deck, the sound of a machine that did not need any of them — and the slate on his hip woke and read the stub: four bodies, one of them a bay number.

"Board says clear to the switch," he said. "Ninety kilometers. Coast lights off the trestle if the air's dry."

Wren stepped up. The tape on her wrists caught the lamp, BAY 4 SHIFT 2, three turns, tight.

Then the slate gave one soft note on Coombs's hip, by itself, with nobody within four meters of it but the dark up the ore line.

Miko sat up. "What was that?"

Coombs looked north for a while. "Nothing on the stub," he said.

"Nothing on the stub," Coombs said again, mostly to the slate, and put the tender out onto the ore line.

The four lamps went behind them and the tarp and the dead rig with the square hole in its dash, and then there was dark on both sides and cold coming up off the ballast. The deck plate took the cold first. The shelf over the motor box didn't, and Miko had found that out inside a minute, sitting on the coolant loop — waste heat off the motor, piped through the shelf on purpose — with her boots braced and her arms round her knees like a woman at a stove.

"Warmest seat on the Interior," she said. "Whoever built this rig liked runners."

"Runners," Coombs said from the deck plate, genial as a lit oven. "That's the coast word for a body that walked off a shift contract with wet boots. I haul you back, the roster feeds you, the bunk's hot, and nobody asks what you did in a tool void." He let that sit. "Offer's open at the switch, lid-hand. Open the whole way down."

"Sell it to somebody who's cold," Rhea said.

"One rule aboard, and it's her rule, not mine." Coombs tapped the dash, where a bar of light in the nose read the top of the rail ahead and told the motor what it had found. "She reads the rail. Reads clear, she starts. Reads blocked, she stops. She don't read weather and she don't read you. You could stand on the shoulder waving both arms with your name in lamps and she'd hold forty right past you."

"A body on the rail?" Miko said.

"Then she stops. Then she starts again in ninety seconds, and you'd want to be off it before that."

Miko already had Rhea's seam knife out, the short thin one for opening cargo wrap without breaking the seal, and was working under the dash lip at a palm-sized plate, four bolts and a gasket.

"Transponder," Rhea said. "Answers a board's hail with a number and a position. Cut it, the rig's nothing to any board on the line."

"Never keyed." Miko tipped the plate into her coat and patted the pocket. "Factory blank. No number, no bay, no owner. That's how he runs a tender that posts nowhere." She lay back on the warm pipe. "There's a woman at Culvert Nine trades flour for a plate with no number on it. Can't trace a blank back to the bay that stamped it."

"She'll trade. She won't hand anything over, and she'll weigh it in front of you."

"Everything's weighed."

Rhea went hunting the brakes, because that was the hole the rule left. If the rig stopped for nothing that wasn't rail, the thing that stopped it was under her hands and she wanted its name. Air first: two reservoirs slung under the deck, a line running forward to the shoes at every wheel, the compressor ticking off the motor. Air shoved the shoes onto the wheels. Lose the air, lose the brakes.

Then, in a bracket behind the motor box, a folding steel arm with a socket on the end, and below it a wedge on a screw, greased, the paint worn off the top where hands had been.

"Reseal," Wren said. She'd come up the deck without Rhea hearing her, tape bright on her wrists. "Bay 4 spur had one. For when the air let go."

"Talk me through it."

"You crank. Screw drives the wedge down till it bites the rail, and friction does the rest." Wren looked at it a moment longer than she needed to. "Forty-two turns."

"Forty-two."

"Then you find out if it's enough."

The crank came out of the bracket heavier than it looked, and the handle was worn bright, the way a tool goes bright when it's used a lot by people in a hurry.

"How many times has this rig needed it?"

Coombs didn't answer that. He was watching the line.

Rhea put her palm flat on the coolant loop to warm it. Hot enough to take skin, nine minutes into a run the board called flat.

"Is she working?"

"She's pulling."

"On the flat?"

"Ore line's all grade," Coombs said. "Some of it's just polite."

Rhea put the crank back in the bracket, within reach of the deck, and left it there. Ahead the gauge sat steady in the green and the rails went into the dark reading clear.
